title: Gender wealth inequality in the European Union: a distributional perspective
summary_en: Are men and women equally wealthy across the EU? Darvas and Ruer use ECB Household Finance and Consumption Survey data 2010–2021 on never-married, dependent-free 25–65-year-olds to isolate the gender wealth gap. Average gaps are statistically insignificant after controlling for demographics, but the picture diverges across the distribution: the middle and upper wealth groups show meaningful, growing gaps. Men hold more property, business assets, and risky financial assets; women hold more bank deposits — and women's educational advantage doesn't translate to wealth.
policy_relevance: Useful for Hungarian and EU gender-equality policy (Magyar Női Lobbi, EMMI, EIGE): supports refocusing the gender-equality agenda from average-wealth measures (which look reassuring) toward the upper distribution and toward the asset-mix channel — pension-asset accumulation, property ownership, investment-account participation. For Hungary, where women's educational advantage is particularly pronounced but pension-savings gaps remain, the paper provides a quantitative benchmark.
